directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Conference sets a reasonable crop on its own but yields much better with a compatible pollinizer such as Comice or Bartlett. The single most widely grown pear in the United Kingdom and one of the most recognizable European pears, it bears reliable, heavy crops of long, tapered, bronze-russeted fruit with sweet, juicy, fine-textured flesh that stores and ships notably well compared to more delicate dessert pear varieties. Its partial self-fertility, reliable heavy cropping, and good disease tolerance compared to some other European pears have made it a standard, forgiving choice for a home orchard, though a second variety nearby still meaningfully boosts yield. Harvest while still firm and green in early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for the characteristic sweet, juicy texture, since pears ripen from the inside out and are best picked underripe from the tree.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Concorde benefits from a compatible pollinizer such as Conference or Comice for best fruit set.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Concorde benefits from a compatible pollinizer such as Conference or Comice for best fruit set. Bred in England from a cross of Conference and the richly flavored Doyenne du Comice, it combines the best traits of both parents, producing long, slender, Conference-shaped fruit with the sweeter, more aromatic dessert flavor of Comice, on a tree that is notably more compact and easier to manage in a home garden than either parent. Its excellent flavor, attractive fruit shape, and good storage life have made it an increasingly popular modern addition to home orchards, particularly where garden space favors a smaller, more manageable tree. Harvest while still firm and green in early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature, since pears ripen best off the tree rather than left to soften on the branch.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Beurre Hardy is a vigorous, reliable tree well suited to a home orchard.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Beurre Hardy is a vigorous, reliable tree well suited to a home orchard. A classic French dessert pear introduced in the early nineteenth century, its name meaning roughly buttery and hardy, it bears attractive bronze-russeted, greenish fruit with exceptionally juicy, melting, sweet flesh carrying a distinctive light rosewater aroma prized by pear connoisseurs, on a notably vigorous, reliably productive, and disease-tolerant tree. Its combination of rich flavor, vigorous growth, and good disease resistance compared to some other classic European pears has kept it in cultivation as a favorite home orchard variety for two centuries. Harvest while still firm and green in late summer to early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for a few days until the flesh yields slightly to gentle pressure near the stem.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett; Packham's Triumph is a vigorous, productive tree valued for reliable cropping.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett; Packham's Triumph is a vigorous, productive tree valued for reliable cropping. Bred in New South Wales, Australia in the nineteenth century from a Bartlett seedling, it has become one of the most important commercial pear varieties in the Southern Hemisphere and a significant global export pear, bearing knobbly, irregular, pale green fruit that ripens to yellow-green with sweet, juicy, Bartlett-like flavor and notably good storage and shipping qualities. Its productive, reliable bearing and adaptability to a somewhat wider climate range than more cold-demanding European pears have made it a valued choice for warmer-winter home orchards seeking a Bartlett-type dessert pear. Harvest while still firm and green in early fall, then ripen indoors at room temperature for the best sweet, juicy dessert texture.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center
